source_metadata.title: Management of Therapeutic-intensity Unfractionated Heparin: A Narrative Review on Critical Points

atoms.canonical_statement: This narrative review revisits fundamental concepts of therapeutic-intensity unfractionated heparin (UFH), organizes unresolved issues into five key points, and identifies priorities for future clinical research.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: In this narrative review, we revisit the fundamental concepts

atoms.canonical_statement: The review frames contemporary therapeutic UFH use as concentrated in selected high-risk groups, including cardiac surgery, intensive care, and severe renal impairment.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: limited to selected patient groups: patients in cardiac surgery

population.label: Patients receiving therapeutic UFH in selected high-risk settings

atoms.canonical_statement: The article is explicitly a narrative review; the source does not report a systematic search strategy, database list, search dates, eligibility criteria, or formal risk-of-bias method.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: In this narrative review

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors define therapeutic dose as UFH doses used for treatment of acute venous thromboembolism and define laboratory monitoring mainly as repeated aPTT or anti-Xa testing used to adjust dose.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: the term “therapeutic dose” refers to doses used for treatment

atoms.canonical_statement: UFH preparations may differ in bulk material and chain-length distribution, and the review states that the half-life is dose dependent, approximately 60 to 90 minutes at usual intravenous doses.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The half-life of UFH is dose-dependent, ranging from 60 to 90 minutes

atoms.canonical_statement: Key point 1: currently used laboratory tests for therapeutic UFH monitoring have important limitations and do not capture all potentially clinically relevant UFH effects.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Laboratory Tests for Unfractionated Heparin Monitoring have Significant Limitations

atoms.canonical_statement: The review states that aPTT and anti-Xa assays do not investigate UFH pleiotropic effects or all antithrombin-independent anticoagulant mechanisms.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: pleiotropic effects of UFH, which may have clinical relevance, are not investigated

atoms.canonical_statement: Because routine aPTT and anti-Xa testing uses platelet-poor plasma, these assays incompletely represent platelet contributions to coagulation and heparin neutralization.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: coagulation tests are performed with platelet-poor plasma and hence miss the role of platelets

atoms.canonical_statement: The aPTT can be prolonged by non-UFH factors such as contact-system defects, some C-reactive-protein/reagent interactions, and lupus anticoagulant, while inflammation-associated high factor VIII can shorten aPTT and reduce apparent UFH sensitivity.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: high factor VIII levels, which are frequent in case of inflammation, shorten the aPTT

atoms.canonical_statement: The review notes that anti-Xa is often considered preferable to aPTT for UFH monitoring despite a lack of robust clinical validation establishing superiority in outcomes.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Despite the lack of robust validation, anti-Xa levels have often been considered a better option

atoms.canonical_statement: The review reports a study in therapeutic-UFH patients in which anti-Xa results differed within the nominal 0.30–0.70 IU/mL therapeutic range in up to 46% of comparisons between BiophenLRT and STA-Liquid anti-Xa reagents.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: discrepancies in anti-Xa levels within the therapeutic range (0.30–0.70 IU/mL) reached up to 46%

concept.text: Discordant anti-Xa classification/value within the therapeutic range

atoms.canonical_statement: The review reports that after protamine neutralization in cardiac surgery, 6% of anti-Xa values measured with dextran-sulfate-containing reagents versus 77% measured without dextran sulfate were below the lower limit of quantification as expected.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: only 6% of anti-Xa values versus 77% were found below the lower limit of quantification

population.label: Patients after protamine neutralization of UFH in cardiac surgery

concept.text: Anti-Xa value below lower limit of quantification

quantitative_result.effect_measure: proportion below lower limit of quantification with dextran sulfate

atoms.canonical_statement: The review identifies dextran sulfate, exogenous antithrombin, collection tube, calibrator, and calibration processing as potential contributors to anti-Xa assay variability.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: other parameters might potentially contribute to disparities in anti-Xa levels

atoms.canonical_statement: Anti-Xa levels do not describe inflammation- or hypercoagulability-related changes in thrombin generation and can therefore dissociate from aPTT.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: anti-Xa levels provide no information about the effect of UFH in case of inflammation and hypercoagulability

atoms.canonical_statement: The review warns that UFH-calibrated anti-Xa assays can detect other Xa inhibitors, creating potential confusion when patients transition from a direct oral Xa inhibitor to UFH.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: potential source of confusion when a patient is switched from a direct oral Xa inhibitor to UFH

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors state that available data are too limited to conclude the clinical implications of choosing aPTT versus anti-Xa monitoring, although anti-Xa monitoring has been associated with faster achievement of a therapeutic range.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: there are too few data to conclude on the clinical implications

atoms.canonical_statement: Table 1 contrasts aPTT as widely available and inexpensive but nonspecific and reagent-sensitive with anti-Xa as less available and more expensive, target-specific, but insufficiently standardized across assays.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Respective advantages/disadvantages of activated partial thromboplastin time and anti-Xa

atoms.canonical_statement: Key point 2: therapeutic ranges used for UFH monitoring are not well grounded in contemporary clinical-outcome validation.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Therapeutic Ranges are not Well Grounded

atoms.canonical_statement: The review states that the widely used anti-Xa target range of 0.30–0.70 IU/mL was established from historical methods and should be viewed skeptically because its relationship to thrombosis and bleeding outcomes remains inadequately validated.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The anti-Xa range from 0.3 to 0.7 IU/mL has been widely accepted for decades

atoms.canonical_statement: The review describes a 1970s prospective study of 234 UFH-treated patients that associated an aPTT ratio of 1.5–2.5 times control with low recurrent-thrombosis risk, using aPTT methods and reagents no longer used.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: prospective study performed in the 1970s with 234 patients

population.label: UFH-treated patients with VTE, myocardial infarction, or arterial thrombosis

concept.text: Recurrent thrombosis risk in relation to aPTT response

quantitative_result.effect_measure: aPTT therapeutic ratio range upper bound

atoms.canonical_statement: The review reports that historical protamine-titration work established a heparin level range of 0.35–0.67 IU/mL, but the anti-Xa reagent used to translate that range is seldom used today and applicability to current assays is unknown.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: enabled the establishment of a heparin level therapeutic range of 0.35 to 0.67 IU/mL

atoms.canonical_statement: In a randomized comparison reported by the review, recurrent VTE occurred in 3/65 anti-Xa-monitored patients and 4/66 aPTT-monitored patients; the reported between-group difference was 1.5% (95% CI −6.7% to 8.4%; p=0.7).

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: 3/65 and 4/66 patients experienced recurrent VTE

population.label: Patients requiring a large daily dose of UFH

quantitative_result.effect_measure: reported between-group difference in recurrent VTE

atoms.canonical_statement: In the same randomized comparison, bleeding events were reported in 1 anti-Xa-monitored patient and 4 aPTT-monitored patients; the reported difference was 4.6% (95% CI −3.3% to 7.5%; p=0.4).

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: There were four bleeding events in the aPTT group and one in the anti-Xa group

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors conclude that no contemporary clinical studies have validated the commonly used 0.30–0.70 IU/mL anti-Xa therapeutic range with currently used anti-Xa assays.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: no clinical studies have challenged the therapeutic range (rounded to 0.3–0.7 IU/mL)

atoms.canonical_statement: The review reports a randomized trial in acute proximal DVT in which an intermittent subcutaneous UFH regimen produced recurrent VTE in 11/57 patients (19.3%) versus 3/58 (5.2%) with continuous IV UFH, with p=0.024.

population.label: Patients with acute proximal deep vein thrombosis

quantitative_result.effect_measure: recurrent VTE proportion with subcutaneous UFH

atoms.canonical_statement: The review reports that a fixed-dose subcutaneous UFH regimen of 250 IU/kg every 12 hours after a 333 IU/kg loading dose was noninferior to twice-daily LMWH for recurrent VTE at 90 days, with rates of 3.8% versus 3.4%.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: fixed dose of 250 IU/kg every 12 hours, preceded by a 333 IU/kg SC loading dose

population.label: Patients in the randomized Fixed-Dose Heparin trial

exposures.details: preceded by 333 IU/kg subcutaneous loading dose

quantitative_result.effect_measure: recurrent VTE proportion with fixed-dose UFH

atoms.canonical_statement: In the Fixed-Dose Heparin trial as reported by the review, major bleeding occurred in 1.1% of the fixed-dose subcutaneous UFH group versus 1.4% of the twice-daily LMWH group.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: major bleeding (1.1 vs. 1.4%)

quantitative_result.effect_measure: major bleeding proportion with fixed-dose UFH

atoms.canonical_statement: The review states that the only identified review/meta-analysis comparing aPTT-guided versus anti-Xa-guided UFH therapy found no clear advantage in bleeding or thrombotic outcomes, but its evidence base was limited and heterogeneous.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: did not show any advantage when comparing aPTT-guided and anti-Xa-guided UFH therapy

atoms.canonical_statement: Key point 3: the influence of endogenous antithrombin levels on UFH anticoagulant activity and patient outcomes is not well established.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The Actual Influence of Antithrombin Levels on Unfractionated Heparin’s Anticoagulant Activity is Not Well Established

atoms.canonical_statement: The review states that the commonly cited antithrombin level of 50 IU/dL as sufficient for heparin effect lacks hard supporting data and that assay-dependent effects have no established threshold.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: no hard data support this assumption

atoms.canonical_statement: Most clinical evidence on antithrombin supplementation comes from cardiac-surgery studies, where randomized trials did not demonstrate improved patient outcomes and raised concerns about bleeding and acute kidney injury.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: randomized controlled trials failed to demonstrate any benefit of AT supplementation on patient outcomes

atoms.canonical_statement: The review argues that thrombin-generation assays suggest a continuous relationship between antithrombin level and thrombin potential without a discernible threshold, while routine aPTT and anti-Xa assays may poorly capture this effect.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: the effect is continuous with no discernible threshold

atoms.canonical_statement: Key point 4: the authors argue that the concept of UFH resistance, as commonly used for high dose requirements or reduced laboratory responsiveness, lacks supporting data and should not be used uncritically.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The Concept of Unfractionated Heparin Resistance Lacks Supporting Data

atoms.canonical_statement: The review distinguishes true pharmacologic failure of heparin at its target from more common apparent reduced responsiveness caused by inter- and intraindividual variability, PF4 release, analytical issues, or acquired antithrombin deficiency.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: rather than to a genuine resistance

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors state that promptly achieving therapeutic UFH levels within 24 hours, especially in acute VTE, is clinically important and that reliable weight-based nomograms with rapid dose adjustment often address apparent reduced responsiveness.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: clinically important to promptly reach therapeutic levels of UFH within 24 hours

atoms.canonical_statement: The review reports that the Raschke randomized trial found more patients reached the aPTT target within 24 hours with a weight-based UFH nomogram, and recurrent thromboembolism was more frequent with standard care (reported relative risk 5; 95% CI 1.1–21.9).

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: relative risk: 5, 95% CI: 1.1–21.9

population.label: Patients in the Raschke randomized UFH nomogram trial

quantitative_result.effect_measure: relative risk for recurrent thromboembolism with standard care versus weight-based nomogram

atoms.canonical_statement: Subsequent tested nomograms, often adapted from Raschke and using anti-Xa targets, generally improved target attainment speed and reduced dose adjustments, but the authors emphasize that these nomograms still require full validation.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: these nomograms require validation

atoms.canonical_statement: When laboratory responsiveness to UFH is reduced, the authors propose coordinated review of preanalytical PF4 release, drug delivery, assay problems, patient factors, appropriate weight-based dosing/monitoring, and possible heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: systematic analysis when facing reduced responsiveness of lab testing to UFH

atoms.canonical_statement: Key point 5: evidence supporting therapeutic UFH dosing and monitoring outside acute venous thromboembolism is scarce and often extrapolated from VTE practice.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Scarce Data are Available on Unfractionated Heparin Use beyond Acute Venous Thromboembolism

atoms.canonical_statement: For acute coronary syndromes, the review notes that lower UFH doses than for VTE have been recommended historically without a specified, well-validated therapeutic monitoring range.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: lower UFH doses than those for VTE are offered for treatment of ACS but without any specified therapeutic range

atoms.canonical_statement: For ECMO, the review describes the evidence base as sparse; it reports studies in which acquired antithrombin deficiency did not correlate with heparin responsiveness, antithrombin supplementation did not improve key clinical outcomes, and anti-Xa monitoring improved precision relative to aPTT in one setting.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Few studies are available on this topic

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors state that they found no data supporting how therapeutic UFH should be used for patients with mechanical heart valves, describing current management as based on clinical experience.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: no data are available supporting the way to use UFH for patients with mechanical heart valves

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors identify three priority research needs: clarify differences among anti-Xa assay formats and the role of dextran sulfate, confirm or reestablish therapeutic UFH ranges using current reagents and clinical outcomes, and fully validate UFH dose-adjustment nomograms.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: the following issues should be appropriately addressed in future clinical research

atoms.canonical_statement: Despite acknowledged limitations, the authors prefer anti-Xa over aPTT for therapeutic UFH monitoring and favor anti-Xa assays without exogenous antithrombin.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: we prefer the use of an anti-Xa assay over aPTT

atoms.canonical_statement: The review concludes that guidance is needed for UFH management, including validated nomograms and clearer specification of monitoring tests and reagents.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Guidance on UFH management including nomograms, tests, and reagents for monitoring is also required

atoms.canonical_statement: Because the article is a narrative review without a reported systematic evidence-selection or risk-of-bias process, its synthesis is vulnerable to selection and interpretation bias and cannot establish comparative effectiveness of monitoring strategies.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: In this narrative review

atoms.canonical_statement: The article discloses consulting/authorship-royalty relationships for A. Cuker and institutional consulting/lecture-fee payments involving Alexandre Mansour; the remaining authors report no conflicts.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Other authors have no conflict of interest

atoms.canonical_statement: Figure 1 visually summarizes the review framework: UFH has overlapping AT-mediated, non-AT-mediated, and pleiotropic effects; platelet-poor and whole-blood monitoring strategies each have limitations; five critical points and three research priorities are highlighted.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Five key points
